scope: Written degree-two allocation theorem, one-sided grid adapter, witnessed whole-beta adapter, arbitrary shared chains and fixed-height costs. Not independent execution certification; excludes the later shared-donor collision note and post-request additional local controls.
clarifications_applied: B counts distinct excluded interval resources.
Beta incidence is a declared witnessed subrelation, not all geometric candidates.
Interior TP tips have BP neighbours on both sides; only far tips have cap exits.
Two-ended collision-free cost explicitly means h2=0.
An extra link exposes an existing resource rather than creating credit.
response:
Verdict: ACCEPTI find no mathematical counterexample to the compensation theorem or to the two frozen adapters under the hypotheses stated in the manuscript. The central allocation theorem is correct, the selected-cap incidence relation has resource degree at most two, the original-beta adapter does not double count whole beta paths, the  $r$ -copy chain has the claimed deficient path incidence and one-link repair, and the fixed-height costs  $4$ ,  $L$ , and  $L+2$  are consistent with the relay geometry.There are a few wording conditions that should be made explicit. They are clarifications of the hypotheses, not reasons to reject the theorem.1. Exact allocation theoremLet  $O(r)\subseteq D$  be the set of distinct demand owners of a resource  $r$ , with  $|O(r)|\le 2$ . A resource seen through two ports of the same demand has  $|O(r)|=1$ , so it is a singly owned resource and contributes one unit.Construct the multigraph whose vertices are demands and whose ordinary edges are the resources with two distinct owners. Resources with one owner are singleton marks at that demand. Zero-owner resources do not belong to any demand component.For a connected component with  $n$  demands:If it is a deficient tree, it has exactly  $n-1$  resources, all ordinary two-owner edges. No injective allocation can pay all  $n$  demands because there are only  $n-1$  resources. Orienting a spanning tree away from a chosen root pays every nonroot demand, so  $n-1$  demands are paid.If it has a singly owned resource, root at its owner. Use the singleton resource for the root and the parent edge for every other vertex.If it has an ordinary cycle, choose an ordinary resource  $e$  outside a spanning tree. Root at an endpoint of  $e$ , pay that root with  $e$ , and pay all other vertices with their parent edges in a spanning tree avoiding  $e$ . Parallel edges are handled in exactly the same way.Therefore every nondeficient component is fully paid, and every deficient tree contributes exactly one unpaid demand. Summing over components gives
$$\max |\text{assigned demands}|=|D|-t,$$
where  $t$  is the number of deficient components.This is an elementary orientation and assignment argument. It does not need, and does not assert, a new general graph-matching theorem.The identity
$$|R|=|D|-t+|Q|$$
is also correct for  $Q$  equal to the resources left unused by a maximum allocation. The individual identities of unused resources matter later; cycles do not create an additional unit of resource credit beyond the resources already counted.2. Selected-cap resource degreeThe selected-cap degree argument is valid under the aligned two-row geometry specified in the document.For one side of one interval, inspect the immediately external column:If it is a TP column, the side has one direct terminal candidate.If it is a BT column, the only possible extended access is through a TP in the next column, in the same physical row as the selected BT mediator. That gives one candidate terminal.These cases are mutually exclusive because the immediately external column cannot be both TP and BT.Thus each side contributes at most one terminal candidate, and an interval with two sides has at most two distinct demand owners. If both sides are accessed by the same virtual alpha path, the resource still has one demand owner, not two.The selected-cap mediator does not create an extra resource. It is an already selected physical site used to expose an existing BB interval.The more explicit version of the same argument is:a BT mediator must have a BB neighbor on one side and a TP neighbor on the other;its orientation and the row of the TP user are then fixed;it cannot simultaneously serve two different selected-cap users.That establishes the required degree-two bound for the candidate-access relation.The exact ledger follows algebraically. If  $D$  is the set of virtual TP–TP demands,  $R$  is the set of unmarked interval resources,  $q$  is the number of unused interval resources in a maximum allocation, and  $t$  is the number of deficient components, then
$$|R|=|D|-t+q.$$
Since  $|R|=L-B$  and  $|D|=\alpha'$ ,
$$S-B
=(L-B)+\beta'-\alpha'
=q+\beta'-t.$$
This identity is exact.It does not imply that  $t\le q+\beta'$  in every grid. The remaining issue is geometric: the unused resources counted by  $q$  need not automatically be accessible to the deficient trees.3. One accessible interval and the failure of the naive local ruleOne accessible unmarked interval is sufficient to pay one demand in the allocation sense. A virtual alpha path does not need both free terminals to have ports if one of its free terminals accesses a resource that is assigned to it.That statement is local. It does not say that one candidate per demand gives a globally injective allocation.The frozen chain gives a precise counterexample to that stronger rule. Take  $r=2$ . After the prescribed internal links:there are two virtual alpha demands  $d_0,d_1$ ;there is one shared unmarked interval  $g_0$ ;both demands can access  $g_0$ ;neither demand has a singly owned candidate resource in the chain graph.Thus
$$O(g_0)=\{d_0,d_1\}.$$
The incidence component is a two-vertex tree with one edge resource. Each demand has an accessible unmarked interval, but the maximum allocation pays only one of the two demands.For general  $r$ , the incidence graph is  $P_r$ , with  $r$  demands and  $r-1$  edge resources, so exactly one demand is unpaid. This is the correct Hall-type obstruction in the present resource language.The target inequality nevertheless remains strictly true:
$$S-B=(3W-9)r>0.$$
For example, with  $W=6,r=2$ ,
$$S-B=18>0.$$
Therefore the chain refutes the candidate rule “one accessible interval for every demand is enough,” while it does not refute  $S\ge B$ . This distinction is essential and is correctly made in the manuscript.4. Original beta-path adapterThe original-beta construction is sound provided its incidence relation is understood as a declared, witnessed subrelation.For each whole original beta path  $b$ , define the set of distinct original alpha owners that have a certified TP–BP link into  $b$ . Require
$$|\operatorname{Owners}(b)|\le 2.$$
The beta path is one resource, even when both of its BP terminals have candidate links. It must never be counted twice merely because both ends are available.The clean formal object is a witnessed incidence
$$(a,b,\tau_a,\tau_b),$$
where  $a$  is an original alpha path,  $b$  is an original beta path,  $\tau_a$  is an alpha TP terminal,  $\tau_b$  is a beta BP terminal, and the pair is joined by a certified horizontal link.An allocation is injective on alpha demands and beta resources. Consequently:distinct allocated alpha demands have disjoint original alpha terminals;distinct allocated beta resources are distinct original beta paths and therefore have disjoint BP terminals;each allocated demand-resource pair uses only one certified link;no alpha owner or beta owner is selected twice.Hence the chosen links form a genuine terminal matching.The phrase “a fixed matching of such terminal links is one sufficient way to supply this list” is stronger than necessary. A global matching of every candidate link is not required. It is enough to declare at most two distinct alpha owners for each beta resource and attach one certified witness link to each incidence. The allocation then chooses at most one link for each matched alpha-beta pair.With  $R$  equal to the union of unmarked interval resources and whole original beta paths,
$$|R|=L-B+\beta.$$
Applying the same allocation theorem to the original alpha demands gives
$$S-B=q-t.$$
This is correct, and it is separate from the virtual-beta identity. The two representations must not be mixed: original beta paths are resources in the pre-cancellation adapter, whereas  $\beta'$  counts virtual beta paths after cancellation.5. Arbitrary- $r$  frozen side-by-side familyThe numerical inventory is consistent.Each copy of  $\operatorname{direct\_family}(W,4)$  has
$$|T|=13,\qquad |M|=W+4.$$
The translated copies have disjoint selected support and disjoint endpoint graphs. The shift by  $8$  preserves the even tile alignment, and the empty column between selected supports prevents new occupied adjacencies. Therefore the old freezing and unique-matching certificates replay independently in every copy.For  $r$  copies,
$$|T|=13r,\qquad |M|=(W+4)r.$$
The compact packet has dimensions
$$(W+2)\times(8r+2).$$
Using the stated definition of  $S$ ,
$$S=(3W-9)r+W+2.$$
The boundary budget is
$$B=W+2,$$
so
$$S-B=(3W-9)r>0.$$
The state assignment gives exactly  $2r$  horizontal cancellation links: $2(r-1)$  links from the right states in the  $r-1$  adjacent copy pairs;one middle-state link at the unused endpoint of the first copy;one middle-state link at the unused endpoint of the last copy.Each copy retains one virtual alpha demand. There are no beta paths. Starting from the five mixed paths per direct-family copy, the  $2r$  links leave  $3r$  mixed paths, so the stated inventory
$$\alpha=r,\qquad \beta=0,\qquad \gamma=3r$$
is consistent.Let  $g_i$  be the singleton interval at global column  $9+8i$ , for  $0\le i<r-1$ . Its two and only two owners are:the right-state free terminal  $TP_{7+8i}$  of copy  $i$ , through  $BT_{8+8i}$ ;the left-state free terminal  $TP_{11+8i}$  of copy  $i+1$ , through  $BT_{10+8i}$ .The middle-state endpoint of the first and last copy has free TP5, with BP neighbors on both sides, so it has no direct or selected-cap access. The remaining interior copies have one left and one right state, giving the two neighboring gap resources.Therefore the demand-resource incidence graph is exactly
$$d_0 \;-\; g_0 \;-\; d_1 \;-\; g_1 \;-\; \cdots \;-\; g_{r-2}\;-\;d_{r-1}.$$
It is a deficient tree with  $r$  demand vertices and  $r-1$  resources. There is no singly owned interval in this component.The extra link
$$(R,5)\text{--}(R,6)$$
in the first copy’s previously middle lower endpoint is disjoint from its existing TP3–BP4 link. It moves that endpoint from free TP5 to free TP7, which accesses the lower BB9 interval in the first copy.That lower BB9 interval is unmarked and singly owned:for  $r=2$ , the second copy’s lower endpoint is middle and has no access;for  $r>2$ , it is right-state, so its access is to its own right gap, not to the first copy’s lower BB9.Thus one can assign
$$d_0\longmapsto \text{newly exposed lower BB9},$$
and assign  $d_{i+1}$  to  $g_i$  for  $0\le i<r-1$ . All  $r$  demands are paid by distinct existing interval resources.The extra link does not create a new interval or new credit. It changes the incidence relation by turning a previously unused interval into a singly owned resource. The ledger changes from
$$S-B=(S-B+1)-1$$
to
$$S-B=(S-B)-0.$$
The remaining other endpoint of the last demand is still unported. That does not matter for the one-resource allocation, and it is exactly why the repair distinguishes one-sided payment from two-ended connector exposure.6. Fixed-height costs  $4$ ,  $L$ , and  $L+2$ For  $\operatorname{relay\_family}(8,4,L,L)$ ,  $L\ge3$ , the stated inventory is consistent:
$$10\times(2L+10),\qquad
|T|=4L+13,\qquad
|M|=2L+14,$$
and
$$S-B=4L+13.$$
The three costs have different meanings.Both endpoints merely accessible:  $4$ Each endpoint can reach its right exit in two horizontal links. Thus both endpoints can be exposed in
$$2+2=4$$
links.Both right exits are boundary-marked. The resulting connector has two boundary marks, so it contributes a twice-marked path,  $h_2=1$ . The value  $4$  is therefore an access cost, not a collision-free compensation cost.One usable unmarked interval:  $L$ The interior TP tips in each relay row have BP neighbors on both sides. They are neither direct TP–BB exits nor TP–BT–BB cap exits. The only unmarked exit is the far left exit.A simple horizontal matching walk cannot reverse through the same gate because it would reuse a terminal. Each crossed relay gate costs one link. Therefore reaching an unmarked interval costs exactly  $L$  links.That one-sided route is enough to allocate one unmarked resource to the demand. The other free endpoint may remain unported.Both endpoints accessible with  $h_2=0$ :  $L+2$ A connector with  $h_2=0$  cannot use both right exits, because that would produce two boundary marks on the same connector path. At least one endpoint must therefore reach a left unmarked exit, costing  $L$ .The other endpoint can reach either the left exit or the right exit. The shortest possible second route is the right route of length  $2$ . Since  $L\ge3$ ,
$$L+2\le 2L,$$
and the lower bound  $L+2$  is attained by one left route and one right route. The two routes lie in different rows, so they do not reuse terminals or interval resources.Thus the three exact costs are:
$$\boxed{
\text{two-ended access}=4,\qquad
\text{one-sided unmarked payment}=L,\qquad
\text{two-ended }h_2=0\text{ access}=L+2.
}$$
The manuscript should use  $h_2=0$  explicitly wherever it says “no twice-marked” or “collision-free,” because “collision-free” could otherwise be read as only a terminal-injectivity condition.7. Clarifications I recommend addingThese do not change the ACCEPT verdict.Define  $B$  as a resource count.The identities using  $L-B$  require  $B$  to be the number of distinct marked interval resources excluded from allocation, or require an explicit hypothesis that each boundary mark corresponds to a different interval resource. In the displayed frozen families this condition holds.Make beta incidence witnessed.State that the beta resource graph uses a selected certified subrelation of alpha-beta terminal links, with at most two distinct alpha owners per whole beta path. Do not interpret the theorem as claiming that every geometrically possible beta neighbor automatically satisfies the degree bound.State the relay exit lemma explicitly.Add the sentence that every interior TP tip has BP neighbors on both sides and hence no direct or selected-cap access, while the only cap exits are the two far tips. This is the geometric fact supporting the  $L$  and  $L+2$  lower bounds.Disambiguate “one extra resource.”In the abstract allocation theorem, adding one resource to a deficient tree is sufficient. In the frozen chain, the extra link does not create a resource; it exposes an already existing unused interval by changing its ownership incidence. The manuscript already explains this correctly in Section 4, and the final verification paragraph should use the same wording.The universal compensation problem remains open. The theorem proves an exact conditional allocation identity and the stated frozen adapters; it does not prove that arbitrary deficient components can always reach distinct unused intervals, nor that  $t\le q+\beta'$  in every frozen grid.
